hints: Focus on what sublimation tells you, a low sublimation temperature points to simple covalent molecules in the vapour, not a giant ionic lattice.
Remember aluminium in $\text{AlCl}_3$ has only 6 electrons in its outer shell, so it wants to accept a lone pair to complete its octet.
Think about how two $\text{AlCl}_3$ units can join by two bridging Cl atoms forming dative bonds, and check the direction the arrows must point.
walkthrough:
**Decide ionic or covalent in the vapour**

Solid aluminium chloride has a layered ionic-like lattice, but it sublimes at only $178^{\circ}\text{C}$. That low temperature tells you the vapour cannot contain separate $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions.

Think covalent, small molecules that can escape easily:
$$\text{solid lattice} \rightarrow \text{covalent molecules (vapour)}$$

**Spot the electron deficiency of aluminium**

In a simple $\text{AlCl}_3$ unit, Al forms 3 covalent bonds and has only 6 outer electrons. It is electron deficient and can accept a lone pair from a Cl atom on a neighbour.

$$\text{Al in AlCl}_3 : 3 \text{ bonds} = 6e^-, \text{needs 2 more for octet}$$

**Build the dimer with bridging chlorines**

At $178^{\circ}\text{C}$ two $\text{AlCl}_3$ molecules join to give $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$. Two Cl atoms become bridges, each forms one normal covalent bond to one Al and one dative bond to the other Al.

$$2\text{AlCl}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$$

**Check the dative arrow directions**

A dative arrow points from donor to acceptor, so from Cl to Al. For symmetry, one bridge donates left to right and the other donates right to left. Each Al ends up tetrahedral with 8 electrons.

This matches the dimer with opposite-pointing Cl to Al arrows, which is the stable vapour species at this temperature.

options.A: Correct. This is the $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dimer. Two $\text{Cl}$ atoms bridge the two Al atoms, each providing one normal bond and one dative bond (Cl to Al). The arrows point in opposite directions so each Al gets one dative bond and achieves an octet with tetrahedral geometry. This is the actual vapour species just above sublimation.
options.B: Incorrect. This also shows an $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ skeleton but the dative arrows are the wrong way round. Both arrows cannot sensibly donate in the way shown, as it would leave one Al still electron deficient and the other with too many electrons. Students choosing this have the right dimer idea but miss the donor to acceptor logic.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the trigonal planar $\text{AlCl}_3$ monomer. The monomer does exist, but only at much higher temperatures (above about $400^{\circ}\text{C}$) when the dimer dissociates. At $178^{\circ}\text{C}$ the dimer is favoured because the extra dative bonds give each Al an octet.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{Al}^{3+}(\text{Cl}^-)_3$ represents separate ions in the solid lattice, not a vapour species. Ions with strong electrostatic attraction do not exist as a gas at only $178^{\circ}\text{C}$. Sublimation produces neutral covalent molecules.
